name: विभूतियोग
teaching: Wherever you find splendour — in rivers the Ganga, in mountains Meru, in speech the single syllable, in the silent the silence — you are seeing a spark of one fire. Krishna lists his glories not as autobiography but as a training of the eye: learn to trace every excellence back to its source. The whole universe stands on a fragment of it. Every splendor in the world is a fingerprint: the catalog of glories trains the eye until one rule suffices — whatever shines anywhere is a spark of one fire. He stands at the heart of all beings, and one fragment of Him sustains everything.
questions: What most recently stopped you with its beauty or power — and did you follow it back to its source?
Among the glories Krishna names are gambling of the dishonest and the rod of punishers. Can you find the sacred even in what disturbs you?
If you listed your own ten glories, what would the list reveal about what you worship?

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
भूय एव महाबाहो शृणु मे परमं वचः ।
यत्तेऽहं प्रीयमाणाय वक्ष्यामि हितकाम्यया॥
verses.transliteration:
bhūya eva mahābāho śṛṇu me paramaṃ vacaḥ
yatte'haṃ prīyamāṇāya vakṣyāmi hitakāmyayā
verses.essence: Again, mighty-armed one, hear my supreme word — which I speak to you, who delight in it, desiring your good.
verses.translation: Again, O mighty-armed Arjuna, listen to my supreme word which I will declare to thee who who art beloved, for thy welfare.

anvaya.parts: महा (great) + बाहु (arm): one whose arms are mighty

anvaya.form: present participle, middle, masculine, dative singular (to one who is delighting)
noun compound, feminine, instrumental singular (out of, by)
anvaya.parts: हित (welfare) + काम्या (wish): out of a wish for your good

verses.explanation: Two reasons the teaching continues past its own summaries: prīyamāṇāya — Arjuna is *enjoying* this, drinking it in — and hita-kāmyayā, the speaker wants his good. Revelation here is not a syllabus to complete but a generosity that keeps overflowing wherever it finds delight.
verses.connection: Reopens the discourse after chapter 9's seal — love of the listener as sufficient cause.
verses.reflection: Stay for the encore today: when you think you have heard it all, love says 'further — listen.'
verses.background: Krishna, unprompted now, continues for the joy of the listener: hear again My supreme word, spoken for your good because you are beloved. Neither gods nor great sages know My origin, for I am their origin; the wise who know Me as unborn Lord are freed — every quality of beings, from intellect to fear and fearlessness, arises from Me alone.
verses.hook: Why does Krishna begin speaking to Arjuna again?

views.text: Paramam vacaḥ is speech that points to the transcendent Reality. Arjuna drinks it in like nectar, and because he so delights in it the Lord keeps speaking for his good.
The renewed teaching widens Arjuna's grasp of the Lord's greatness and tells how devotion arises and grows. The Lord speaks both because Arjuna enjoys hearing and because the Lord loves him.
The glories shown briefly in chapters 7 to 9 are now spread out in detail, so that the Lord may be seen everywhere. Mahābāho means one whose arms are skilled in his own duty or in serving the great.
Pleased by Arjun's eager interest, Krishna resolves to describe His glories to deepen Arjun's joy and devotion, treating him as a beloved confidant.

verses.devanagari:
न मे विदुः सुरगणाः प्रभवं न महर्षयः ।
अहमादिर्हि देवानां महर्षीणां च सर्वशः॥
verses.transliteration:
na me viduḥ suragaṇāḥ prabhavaṃ na maharṣayaḥ
ahamādirhi devānāṃ maharṣīṇāṃ ca sarvaśaḥ
verses.essence: Neither the hosts of gods nor the great sages know my origin — for I am, in every way, the source of the gods and the great sages.
verses.translation: Neither the hosts of the gods nor the great sages know My origin; for in every way I am the source of all the gods and the great sages.

anvaya.form: verb, perfect form with present sense, 3rd person plural

anvaya.parts: सुर (god) + गण (host): the hosts of the gods
महा (great) + ऋषि (seer): the great seers
महा (great) + ऋषि (seer)

verses.explanation: The epistemological ceiling: even the highest created knowers cannot see behind their own beginning — the lamp cannot stand behind its own light. Whatever gods and seers report of him is testimony from downstream; the source remains upstream of every witness.
verses.connection: Sets the limit that makes 10.3's knower so rare: God's origin is structurally unwitnessable.
verses.reflection: Respect the mystery's depth: even the gods cannot trace His origin. Let your not-knowing relax.
verses.background: Krishna, unprompted now, continues for the joy of the listener: hear again My supreme word, spoken for your good because you are beloved. Neither gods nor great sages know My origin, for I am their origin; the wise who know Me as unborn Lord are freed — every quality of beings, from intellect to fear and fearlessness, arises from Me alone.
verses.hook: Why can't even gods and great sages know God's origin?

refs.note: The gods cannot reach God because He existed before them, which is the verse's reason why they do not know His origin.
The gods came after creation, so who can know where it came from, echoing the verse's point about divine beings.

views.text: Prabhava can be read two ways: his lordly majesty, the fullness of his power, or his coming-into-being, his origin. Either way, even Brahmā and the great seers such as Bhṛgu do not know it.

Whatever the gods and seers know was itself given them by the Lord according to their merit, so it is limited. They cannot grasp his name, deeds, nature and qualities, because he is the source of their very knowledge.
Prabhava is his appearing in many glorious forms though he is unborn. He brings the gods and sages into being and moves their minds, so no one knows him without his grace.
As a son cannot know his father's birth, the gods and sages, born after God, cannot grasp His origin; yet Krishna now reveals this to nurture His friend's devotion.

verses.devanagari:
यो मामजमनादिं च वेत्ति लोकमहेश्वरम् ।
असम्मूढः स मर्त्येषु सर्वपापैः प्रमुच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
yo māmajamanādiṃ ca vetti lokamaheśvaram
asammūḍhaḥ sa martyeṣu sarvapāpaiḥ pramucyate
verses.essence: One who knows me as unborn, beginningless, the great Lord of the worlds — that one, undeluded among mortals, is released from all sins.
verses.translation: He who knows Me as unborn and beginningless, as the great Lord of the worlds, he, among mortals, is undeluded and he is liberated from all sins.

anvaya.parts: अन् (without) + आदि (beginning): that which has no beginning
लोक (world) + महा (great) + ईश्वर (lord): the great lord of the worlds

anvaya.form: adjective, masculine, nominative singular (describing the subject)
noun compound, neuter, instrumental plural (here: from)
anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + पाप (sin): all sins

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is freed)

verses.explanation: What cannot be known by inspection (10.2) can be known by recognition: ajam, anādim, the one who never began. The verse's strange economics returns from 4.36: this single accurate recognition unbinds *all* sins — because sin's root is misplacing the center of the world, and this knowledge places it.
verses.connection: The human counterpart to 10.2's divine unknowability: right relation substitutes for impossible inspection.
verses.reflection: Know one thing greatly today — the unborn, beginningless Lord — and watch lesser confusions release.
verses.background: Krishna, unprompted now, continues for the joy of the listener: hear again My supreme word, spoken for your good because you are beloved. Neither gods nor great sages know My origin, for I am their origin; the wise who know Me as unborn Lord are freed — every quality of beings, from intellect to fear and fearlessness, arises from Me alone.
verses.hook: What frees a person from delusion and sin?

refs.note: God is the supreme controller of all controllers and God of all gods, matching the verse's title for Him as great Lord of the worlds.

views.text: Nothing precedes him as a source, so he is beginningless, and having no origin is why he is unborn. Knowing him so frees one from sins done knowingly or unknowingly.

'Unborn' sets him apart from matter and from bound souls; 'beginningless' sets him apart even from freed souls, whose freedom had a start. Delusion means taking him as one more being of the same kind.
The undeluded person knows his innermost Self is not other than the Supreme. Ignorance, the root of sin, goes, and old impressions are burnt like roasted seeds that cannot sprout.
No one knows God by their own effort, yet those He graces do; knowing Him as the unborn Lord of all frees them from delusion and the reactions of their actions.

verses.devanagari:
बुद्धिर्ज्ञानमसम्मोहः क्षमा सत्यं दमः शमः ।
सुखं दुःखं भवोऽभावो भयं चाभयमेव च॥
verses.transliteration:
buddhirjñānamasammohaḥ kṣamā satyaṃ damaḥ śamaḥ
sukhaṃ duḥkhaṃ bhavo'bhāvo bhayaṃ cābhayameva ca
verses.essence: Understanding, knowledge, freedom from delusion, patience, truth, restraint, calm; pleasure and pain, becoming and ceasing, fear and fearlessness —
verses.translation: Intellect, wisdom, non-delusion, forgiveness, truth, self-restraint, calmness, happiness, pain, existence or birth, non-existence or death, fear and also fearlessness.
verses.explanation: An inventory of the inner weather begins — and it deliberately mixes columns: wisdom beside pain, truth beside fear. Whatever a human being can be or feel, the list is gathering it all toward one source. No state of mind, it will claim, is self-made.
verses.connection: First half of the human-condition catalogue completed in 10.5.
verses.reflection: Notice today's inner weather — clarity, patience, truth, even fear — and read the watermark: from Him.
verses.background: Krishna, unprompted now, continues for the joy of the listener: hear again My supreme word, spoken for your good because you are beloved. Neither gods nor great sages know My origin, for I am their origin; the wise who know Me as unborn Lord are freed — every quality of beings, from intellect to fear and fearlessness, arises from Me alone.
verses.hook: Where do our good and bad qualities and feelings come from?

views.text: Every item is a working of the mind. So bhava and abhava are read as elation and depression, the moods of agreeable and disagreeable experience, rather than birth and death.
These three verses spell out what 'great Lord of the worlds' means. Buddhi is skill in telling the essential from the worthless; their verb comes in 10.5: all these arise from me.
Patience means bearing without complaint the three kinds of suffering: from one's own body, from nature, and from other creatures. It also means wishing no harm to those who abuse you.
All human qualities and emotions come from God, like one electric supply making light, sound or heat in different devices; how His energy shows in us depends on our own free choices.

verses.devanagari:
अहिंसा समता तुष्टिस्तपो दानं यशोऽयशः ।
भवन्ति भावा भूतानां मत्त एव पृथग्विधाः॥
verses.transliteration:
ahiṃsā samatā tuṣṭistapo dānaṃ yaśo'yaśaḥ
bhavanti bhāvā bhūtānāṃ matta eva pṛthagvidhāḥ
verses.essence: — non-injury, equanimity, contentment, austerity, charity, fame and infamy: these manifold states of beings arise from me alone.
verses.translation: Non-injury, equanimity, contentment, austerity, beneficence, fame, ill-fame (these) different kinds of qualities of beings arise from Me alone.

anvaya.parts: पृथक् (separate) + विधा (kind): of separate kinds

verses.explanation: The catalogue closes on its point: matta eva, from me alone — courage and cowardice, honor and disgrace, all drawn from one well at different depths. Nothing in the psyche is foreign territory to him; even the states we are ashamed of are made of borrowed being.
verses.connection: Seals 10.4–5: the whole interior life sourced — preparing the outer-world catalogue to come.
verses.reflection: Trace one quality you prize in yourself to its source, and hold it more lightly, more gratefully.
verses.background: Krishna, unprompted now, continues for the joy of the listener: hear again My supreme word, spoken for your good because you are beloved. Neither gods nor great sages know My origin, for I am their origin; the wise who know Me as unborn Lord are freed — every quality of beings, from intellect to fear and fearlessness, arises from Me alone.
verses.hook: Do even fame, infamy and contentment come from the same source?

views.text: None of these dispositions could exist apart from the Self. They come from God, but to each being in keeping with its own past actions.
Not only the virtues listed but their opposites as well, dullness, delusion and the rest, arise from the Lord alone.
Contentment makes a person rich, while greed makes even a rich man a beggar. True giving is to a worthy person at the right place and time, especially to one who cannot repay.
These dispositions too, from non-violence and equanimity to fame and infamy, arise only to the extent God sanctions; His one energy manifests well or badly in each person according to their actions.

verses.devanagari:
महर्षयः सप्त पूर्वे चत्वारो मनवस्तथा ।
मद्भावा मानसा जाता येषां लोक इमाः प्रजाः॥
verses.transliteration:
maharṣayaḥ sapta pūrve catvāro manavastathā
madbhāvā mānasā jātā yeṣāṃ loka imāḥ prajāḥ
verses.essence: The seven great sages of old, and the four, and the Manus — beings of my nature, born of my mind — from whom all these creatures in the world descend.
verses.translation: The seven great sages, the ancient four and also the Manus, possessed of powers like Me (on account of their minds being fixed on Me), were born of (My) mind; from them are these creatures born in this world.

anvaya.parts: महा (great) + ऋषि (seer)
मत् (me) + भाव (nature): those whose nature or power is mine

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, nominative plural (were born)
relative pronoun, masculine, genitive plural (of whom)

verses.explanation: Genealogy compressed: the seven seers, the four primordial ones, the Manus — humanity's traditional founding fathers — were themselves mānasāḥ, thought into being, mind-born of him. Trace any family tree far enough and it roots not in soil but in a meditation.
verses.connection: Extends the sourcing from inner states (10.4–5) to the human lineage itself.
verses.reflection: Honor the ancient lineage you stand in — every teacher's teacher traces to one mind.
verses.background: Krishna, unprompted now, continues for the joy of the listener: hear again My supreme word, spoken for your good because you are beloved. Neither gods nor great sages know My origin, for I am their origin; the wise who know Me as unborn Lord are freed — every quality of beings, from intellect to fear and fearlessness, arises from Me alone.
verses.hook: Where did the first sages and progenitors of humanity come from?

views.text: The four are four Manus, the Sāvarṇas. Madbhāvāḥ means their thoughts were fixed on him, and so they were endowed with Viṣṇu's power; they were created by his mind alone.
The seers carry creation forward and the Manus sustain it until dissolution. Their disposition is his own: they live by his will.
The four are Sanaka and his brothers, older still than the seven seers. All arose by the mere resolve of his mind as Hiraṇyagarbha, and their 'offspring' include both sons and disciples.
Through the four Kumars, seven sages and fourteen Manus, all born from Brahma, who comes from Vishnu, an expansion of Krishna, he traces all beings back to Krishna as the original forefather.

verses.devanagari:
एतां विभूतिं योगं च मम यो वेत्ति तत्त्वतः ।
सोऽविकम्पेन योगेन युज्यते नात्र संशयः॥
verses.transliteration:
etāṃ vibhūtiṃ yogaṃ ca mama yo vetti tattvataḥ
so'vikampena yogena yujyate nātra saṃśayaḥ
verses.essence: One who knows in truth this pervading power and yoga of mine is harnessed in unshakable yoga — of this there is no doubt.
verses.translation: He who in truth knows these manifold manifestations of My Being and (this) Yoga-power of Mine becomes established in the unshakable Yoga; there is no doubt about it.

anvaya.form: verb, passive, present, 3rd person singular (is joined)

verses.explanation: The chapter's keyword arrives: vibhūti — the pervading manifestation, the glory-in-things. Knowing it tattvataḥ produces avikampa yoga, a union that no longer trembles: a vision of God braided through everything cannot be dislodged by any one thing going wrong.
verses.connection: Names the chapter's subject and its fruit: steadiness purchased by seeing him everywhere.
verses.reflection: Let conviction in this glory steady you once today — unwavering yoga begins as settled knowing.
verses.background: Krishna, unprompted now, continues for the joy of the listener: hear again My supreme word, spoken for your good because you are beloved. Neither gods nor great sages know My origin, for I am their origin; the wise who know Me as unborn Lord are freed — every quality of beings, from intellect to fear and fearlessness, arises from Me alone.
verses.hook: What happens to one who truly knows God's glories and power?

views.text: Vibhūti is his all-pervasiveness and yoga his power to accomplish anything. Knowing these, one gains unwavering yoga: steadiness in perfect knowledge.
To know that all origin, sustenance and activity depend on him, and that his yoga is his host of auspicious qualities, makes bhakti unshakable. Knowledge of his glory feeds devotion.
Whoever truly sees this beholds the Lord in all beings and hates no creature. Feelings of superiority and inferiority fall away, and balance holds in any circumstance.
Knowledge of God's greatness feeds love, as learning a stone's sacred history deepens one's regard for it; those convinced of His glory naturally turn to steady devotion.

verses.devanagari:
अहं सर्वस्य प्रभवो मत्तः सर्वं प्रवर्तते ।
इति मत्वा भजन्ते मां बुधा भावसमन्विताः॥
verses.transliteration:
ahaṃ sarvasya prabhavo mattaḥ sarvaṃ pravartate
iti matvā bhajante māṃ budhā bhāvasamanvitāḥ
verses.essence: I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds. Realizing this, the wise worship me, filled with loving feeling.
verses.translation: I am the source of all; from Me everything evolves; understanding thus, the wise, endowed with meditation, worship Me.

anvaya.parts: भाव (feeling, love) + समन्वित (endowed with): those filled with feeling

verses.explanation: First of four verses (10.8–11) that Śrīdhara reads as one unit and that Gaudiya devotion treasures as the chatuh-shloki, the Gita's seed within the Gita. The metaphysics fits in one line: aham sarvasya prabhavo, mattaḥ sarvaṁ pravartate — I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds. The second line shows what metaphysics is *for*: iti matvā — having truly absorbed it — the wise do not merely conclude; they worship, bhāva-samanvitāḥ, filled with feeling. Understood origin becomes overflowing love; thought completes itself as devotion.
verses.connection: Opens the chatuh-shloki (10.8–11), the four verses many call the whole Gita in miniature.
verses.reflection: Say the seed-verse once with feeling: He is the origin of all; from Him everything proceeds.
verses.background: Four verses the tradition treasures as the Gita's seed: I am the source of all, from Me all proceeds — the wise worship Me with feeling; their minds and lives in Me, they delight in speaking of Me; to these ever-yoked lovers I give the yoga of understanding; dwelling in their own hearts, I destroy their darkness with the lamp of knowledge.
verses.hook: What understanding moves the wise to worship God?

refs.note: The divine says it makes those it loves mighty, wise and even fit to be Brahma, supporting the claim that everything comes from God.
All forms of God are expansions of Krishna, the original form, supporting His claim to be the source of all.
Countless universes arise from Maha Vishnu's breath, and Maha Vishnu is a part of Govinda, the original person.

views.text: The 'I' is the supreme Brahman called Vāsudeva. Bhāva means bhāvanā, an ardent longing for the supreme Reality, and the wise who know this adore him with it.
The wise know not only his sovereignty but his tender qualities: condescension, beauty, a parent's affection. Bhāva is a loving disposition, so they worship with intense yearning of the heart.
This verse opens a group of four showing how knowing his glory and power ripens into right knowledge. Bhāva here simply means love (prīti).
Krishna is the cause of all causes, the source of every divine form; He governs creation through His Vishnu expansions while His own play is with liberated souls in His abode.

verses.devanagari:
मच्चित्ता मद्गतप्राणा बोधयन्तः परस्परम् ।
कथयन्तश्च मां नित्यं तुष्यन्ति च रमन्ति च॥
verses.transliteration:
maccittā madgataprāṇā bodhayantaḥ parasparam
kathayantaśca māṃ nityaṃ tuṣyanti ca ramanti ca
verses.essence: With minds in me, with lives surrendered to me, enlightening one another and speaking of me always — they are content, and they rejoice.
verses.translation: With their mind and their life wholly absorbed in Me, enlightening each other and ever speaking of Me, they are satisfied and delighted.

anvaya.parts: मत् (me) + चित्त (mind): those whose minds are in me
मत् (me) + गत (gone) + प्राण (life-breath): those whose life has gone into me

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, nominative plural (while teaching)
present participle, masculine, nominative plural (while speaking)

verses.explanation: The lovers' commune: mac-cittā mad-gata-prāṇāḥ, hearts and very breath relocated into him. Then the verse's warmth: bodhayantaḥ parasparam, teaching *each other*, no hierarchy, the talk of him passing around like bread. This is the satsang verse, the warrant for every circle that ever sat down to speak of God. The closing words are the proof: tuṣyanti ca ramanti ca. This life satisfies *and* delights; Śrīdhara reads the first verb as contentment and the second as deep fulfilment. Devotion's secret is that it is enjoyable.
verses.connection: The community portrait inside the four core verses: shared remembrance as continuous feast.
verses.reflection: Spend ten minutes in the satsang of 10.9: thinking of Him, speaking of Him — and notice the contentment.
verses.background: Four verses the tradition treasures as the Gita's seed: I am the source of all, from Me all proceeds — the wise worship Me with feeling; their minds and lives in Me, they delight in speaking of Me; to these ever-yoked lovers I give the yoga of understanding; dwelling in their own hearts, I destroy their darkness with the lamp of knowledge.
verses.hook: What fills the days and conversations of those devoted to God?

views.text: Mad-gata-prāṇāḥ can also mean that their senses, the eyes and the rest, are withdrawn into him. They rejoice as one does in the company of someone dear.
Their life is centred on him in the sense that they cannot sustain themselves without him. The speakers delight in their own unforced speech, and the listeners find it incomparably dear.
They enlighten each other with reasoned proofs from scripture and sing his praise. Approving one another brings contentment, and that leads to deep fulfilment.
Devotees give their minds and lives to God, accept every situation as His will, and find delight in hearing, speaking and singing of Him, which enlightens others too.

verses.devanagari:
तेषां सततयुक्तानां भजतां प्रीतिपूर्वकम् ।
ददामि बुद्धियोगं तं येन मामुपयान्ति ते॥
verses.transliteration:
teṣāṃ satatayuktānāṃ bhajatāṃ prītipūrvakam
dadāmi buddhiyogaṃ taṃ yena māmupayānti te
verses.essence: To these, ever harnessed, worshiping with love, I give the yoga of understanding by which they come to me.
verses.translation: To them who are ever steadfast, worshipping Me with love, I give the Yoga of discrimination by which they come to Me.

anvaya.form: pronoun, masculine, genitive plural (here: to them)

anvaya.parts: सतत (constant) + युक्त (yoked, joined): those always joined to me

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, genitive plural (of those worshipping)

anvaya.parts: प्रीति (love) + पूर्वक (preceded by): done with love
बुद्धि (understanding) + योग (yoga): the discipline of understanding

anvaya.form: relative pronoun, masculine, instrumental singular (by which)

verses.explanation: The direction of the decisive gift reverses: dadāmi — *I give*. To those constantly yoked, satata-yuktānām, who worship with love, he grants the buddhi-yoga by which they come to him. The understanding that finally carries one home is not built at the summit of effort; it is bestowed midway into love. Prīti-pūrvakam is the trigger: where worship has become affection, the inner teacher takes over the curriculum.
verses.connection: The grace-verse of the four: human love ascends, divine intelligence descends to meet it.
verses.reflection: Practice with love today and expect the inside gift: the buddhi-yoga by which one comes to Him.
verses.background: Four verses the tradition treasures as the Gita's seed: I am the source of all, from Me all proceeds — the wise worship Me with feeling; their minds and lives in Me, they delight in speaking of Me; to these ever-yoked lovers I give the yoga of understanding; dwelling in their own hearts, I destroy their darkness with the lamp of knowledge.
verses.hook: How do devoted people gain the understanding that brings them to God?

refs.note: Those who think they grasp God with the intellect do not; those who know He is beyond it understand, supporting the need for His gift.
The self is described only as 'not this, not this' and cannot be grasped by intellectual effort.
No one can know God without the grace flowing from His feet, which this verse says He gives to devotees.

views.text: Buddhi is full enlightenment about his real nature, and by it they reach him as their own Self. They worship from love, not to gain possessions.
Buddhi-yoga is the matured state of devotion itself. To those who long for unbroken union with him, he gives that devotion lovingly, and by it they come to him.
Buddhi is the inner eye of intuition that sees the One in all as one's own Self in deep meditation, so this buddhi-yoga is jñāna-yoga, given by grace.
The intellect is material and cannot reach God; He Himself gives divine knowledge, not at whim, but to those who unite their minds with Him in loving devotion.

verses.devanagari:
तेषामेवानुकम्पार्थमहमज्ञानजं तमः ।
नाशयाम्यात्मभावस्थो ज्ञानदीपेन भास्वता॥
verses.transliteration:
teṣāmevānukampārthamahamajñānajaṃ tamaḥ
nāśayāmyātmabhāvastho jñānadīpena bhāsvatā
verses.essence: Out of compassion for them, dwelling in their own hearts, I destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge.
verses.translation: Out of mere compassion for them, I, dwelling within their Self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance by the luminous lamp of knowledge.

anvaya.parts: अनुकम्पा (compassion) + अर्थम् (for the sake of): for compassion's sake
अज्ञान (ignorance) + ज (born): what is born of ignorance
आत्मभाव (their inner being) + स्थ (abiding): dwelling within them

anvaya.form: noun compound, masculine, instrumental singular (with, by)
anvaya.parts: ज्ञान (knowledge) + दीप (lamp): the lamp that is knowledge

verses.explanation: Where the gift of 10.10 is delivered from: ātma-bhāva-sthaḥ, stationed within their own inner being, not shouting from a heaven. Anukampā is compassion, literally a trembling-along-with. Out of that compassion alone he destroys the darkness born of ignorance with the shining lamp of knowledge. The image completes the chapter's interior turn: the divine does not hand the devotee a lamp; he *becomes* the lamp, lit from inside the very room that was dark. Grace here is not intervention from above but light from the room's own centre.
verses.connection: Closes the four core verses: the whole drama of liberation relocated to within the lover's own heart.
verses.reflection: Ask once for the lamp, not the map — the indwelling light that destroys darkness at its station.
verses.background: Four verses the tradition treasures as the Gita's seed: I am the source of all, from Me all proceeds — the wise worship Me with feeling; their minds and lives in Me, they delight in speaking of Me; to these ever-yoked lovers I give the yoga of understanding; dwelling in their own hearts, I destroy their darkness with the lamp of knowledge.
verses.hook: How does God remove the darkness of ignorance within?

refs.note: Divine knowledge comes only by God's special grace, which is the lamp of knowledge this verse describes.

views.text: The lamp sits in the heart. It is fed by the oil of grace that comes from devotion, fanned by intense meditation, its wick an intellect purified by discipline, sheltered in a mind free of likes and dislikes.
He abides as the object of their thought and reveals his auspicious qualities through knowledge of himself. The darkness he removes is old karma: the habit of clinging to things other than him.
Through teaching one another, a shock of insight passes between the devotees: all knowing subjects are one Lord. Seeing this, they recognise their own Self as all-powerful and all-pervading.
By grace God gives His divine energy, making the soul's senses, mind and intellect divine; with these it can see and know Him, and the darkness of ignorance is dispelled.

verses.speaker: अर्जुन उवाच
verses.devanagari:
परं ब्रह्म परं धाम पवित्रं परमं भवान् ।
पुरुषं शाश्वतं दिव्यमादिदेवमजं विभुम्॥
verses.transliteration:
paraṃ brahma paraṃ dhāma pavitraṃ paramaṃ bhavān
puruṣaṃ śāśvataṃ divyamādidevamajaṃ vibhum
verses.essence: Arjuna says: You are the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the supreme purifier — the eternal divine Purusha, the primal god, unborn, all-pervading.
verses.translation: Thou art the Supreme Brahman, the supreme abode (or the supreme light), the supreme purifier, eternal, divine Person, the primeval God, unborn and omnipresent.

anvaya.form: pronoun, masculine, nominative singular (subject; takes a 3rd-person verb)
noun, masculine, accusative singular (object of 'declare' in 10.13)

anvaya.parts: आदि (first) + देव (god): the god before all gods

verses.explanation: Arjuna can hold silence no longer; the four verses have lit him, and his answer is a cascade of the tradition's highest titles, poured out in one breath. Notice the movement: the teaching of 10.8–11 was received not as information but as presence, and presence demands address, not notes.
verses.connection: Arjuna's response to the chatuh-shloki: theology turning, mid-sentence, into praise.
verses.reflection: Praise before petitioning today: name the highest as highest, and feel your own scale correct itself.
verses.background: Arjuna responds — the first time in the poem he confesses full faith: You are the supreme Brahman, declared so by Narada, Asita, Devala, Vyasa, and now by Yourself; neither gods nor demons know Your manifestation. Then the request that shapes the chapter: tell me Your divine glories, by which You pervade the worlds — for I am never sated of hearing.
verses.hook: How does Arjuna now describe Krishna after hearing His teaching?

refs.note: Sages including Narada, Markandeya, Bhrigu, Vyasa and Angira praise Krishna as creator and God of gods, the same titles Arjuna gives here.

views.text: Param brahma is the supreme Self. Vibhu, all-pervading, also means one able to take on many forms.

Each title echoes the Upanishads: Brahman is that from which beings arise, dhāman means light, the Light of lights, and he purifies by destroying the meditator's sins without trace. The Nārāyaṇa texts name him all three.
'Supreme' marks the pure, attributeless Absolute, distinct from Brahman with attributes worshipped by devotees. Holy rivers remove sins, but the Supreme destroys ignorance itself, the root of sin.
Arjun rejects the view that avatars are a step removed from God and declares that Krishna in His personal form is the Supreme, the cause of all causes.

verses.devanagari:
आहुस्त्वामृषयः सर्वे देवर्षिर्नारदस्तथा ।
असितो देवलो व्यासः स्वयं चैव ब्रवीषि मे॥
verses.transliteration:
āhustvāmṛṣayaḥ sarve devarṣirnāradastathā
asito devalo vyāsaḥ svayaṃ caiva bravīṣi me
verses.essence: So declare all the sages — the divine sage Narada, Asita, Devala, Vyasa — and you yourself declare it to me.
verses.translation: All the sages have thus declared Thee, as also the divine sage Narada; so also Asita, Devala and Vyasa; and now Thou Thyself sayest so to me.

anvaya.form: verb, perfect form with present sense, 3rd person plural

anvaya.parts: देव (divine) + ऋषि (seer): a seer among the gods

verses.explanation: Arjuna cites his sources like a careful witness: the consensus of the seers, the most venerated names — and then the testimony that outranks them all: svayaṁ caiva bravīṣi me, you yourself are telling me. Tradition corroborates; the living voice confirms. Faith, here, is not a leap but a convergence.
verses.connection: Grounds 10.12's outburst: revelation cross-checked against the whole lineage of seers.
verses.reflection: Borrow the seers' testimony when yours wavers — Narada, Vyasa, and the chain of those who saw.
verses.background: Arjuna responds — the first time in the poem he confesses full faith: You are the supreme Brahman, declared so by Narada, Asita, Devala, Vyasa, and now by Yourself; neither gods nor demons know Your manifestation. Then the request that shapes the chapter: tell me Your divine glories, by which You pervade the worlds — for I am never sated of hearing.
verses.hook: Which sages had already declared Krishna's divinity before Arjuna?

refs.note: Narada, Markandeya, Vyasa and other sages praise Krishna as creator of the worlds and Lord of the gods.
Asita and Devala declare Krishna the creator of Brahma, who creates the three worlds.

views.text: Arjuna repeats the titles the sages give the Lord: eternal divine Person, the primal God who preceded all gods, birthless, and omnipresent, with 'vibhu' glossed as able to assume diverse forms.
The sages are those who know both the higher truth and the lower. Passages from the Mahābhārata have these very seers declare that Kṛṣṇa is Nārāyaṇa himself, come down to Mathurā.
Spiritual truth is established by great authorities, so Arjun cites sages like Narada, Asita, Devala and Vyasa who proclaimed Krishna supreme, and notes Krishna now confirms it Himself.

verses.devanagari:
सर्वमेतदृतं मन्ये यन्मां वदसि केशव ।
न हि ते भगवन्व्यक्तिं विदुर्देवा न दानवाः॥
verses.transliteration:
sarvametadṛtaṃ manye yanmāṃ vadasi keśava
na hi te bhagavanvyaktiṃ vidurdevā na dānavāḥ
verses.essence: All this that you tell me, Keshava, I hold to be true. Indeed, Lord, neither the gods nor the danavas know your manifestation.
verses.translation: I believe all this that Thou sayest to me to be true, O Krishna; verily, O blessed Lord! neither the gods nor the demons know Thy manifestation (origin).

anvaya.form: verb, perfect form with present sense, 3rd person plural

verses.explanation: The word Arjuna chooses is ancient and exact: ṛtam — not merely accurate but true the way cosmic order is true. And he has absorbed 10.2's lesson: if neither gods nor their rivals can see behind the source, then the source's own self-disclosure is the only possible window — and he is standing at it.
verses.connection: Arjuna's act of faith stated formally — acceptance grounded in 10.2's logic of testimony.
verses.reflection: Accept one truth today on the speaker's authority, where neither gods nor demons could verify it.
verses.background: Arjuna responds — the first time in the poem he confesses full faith: You are the supreme Brahman, declared so by Narada, Asita, Devala, Vyasa, and now by Yourself; neither gods nor demons know Your manifestation. Then the request that shapes the chapter: tell me Your divine glories, by which You pervade the worlds — for I am never sated of hearing.
verses.hook: Does Arjuna accept Krishna's words as true, or as metaphor?

refs.note: Bhagavān means one who possesses six opulences without limit, which is why finite gods and demons cannot grasp Him.

views.text: Arjuna accepts as true all that the sages and Krishna have said; neither gods nor demons comprehend his glory (vyakti), since he is the origin of the gods and the rest.
Ṛtam means a statement of things as they really are, not an exaggeration. Vyakti is the way he manifests himself, beyond the limited knowledge of gods and demons.
Arjuna's doubts about the Lord's sovereignty are now gone. The gods do not know that this appearance is to favour them, nor the demons that it is to subdue them.
Bhagavān is one in whom six excellences are complete: wisdom, dispassion, lordship, virtue, fortune and strength. Arjuna calls him Keśava because the Lord knows what is in his mind.
Arjun affirms that everything Krishna taught from the seventh chapter on is literal truth, and calls Him Bhagavān, whose infinite opulences no finite being, god or demon, can comprehend.

verses.devanagari:
स्वयमेवात्मनात्मानं वेत्थ त्वं पुरुषोत्तम ।
भूतभावन भूतेश देवदेव जगत्पते॥
verses.transliteration:
svayamevātmanātmānaṃ vettha tvaṃ puruṣottama
bhūtabhāvana bhūteśa devadeva jagatpate
verses.essence: You alone know yourself by yourself, Purushottama — source of beings, Lord of beings, God of gods, Master of the universe.
verses.translation: Verily, Thou Thyself knowest Thyself by Thyself, O Supreme Person, O source and Lord of all beings, O God of gods, O ruler of the world!

anvaya.form: verb, perfect form with present sense, 2nd person singular

anvaya.parts: पुरुष (person) + उत्तम (highest): the highest of persons
भूत (beings) + भावन (one who brings into being): creator of beings
भूत (beings) + ईश (lord): ruler of beings
देव (god) + देव (god): the god whom the gods worship
जगत् (world) + पति (lord, protector): master of the world

verses.explanation: The epistemology completed: svayam evātmanātmānam — self knowing self by self, the one knowledge with no outside vantage and no instrument but its own light. Hence the request that follows is the only rational move left: if you alone hold the map, unroll it for me.
verses.connection: Sets up 10.16's petition: since self-knowledge of God is God's monopoly, disclosure must be asked for.
verses.reflection: Rest in this: You alone know Yourself by Yourself. Stand at the edge of that and bow.
verses.background: Arjuna responds — the first time in the poem he confesses full faith: You are the supreme Brahman, declared so by Narada, Asita, Devala, Vyasa, and now by Yourself; neither gods nor demons know Your manifestation. Then the request that shapes the chapter: tell me Your divine glories, by which You pervade the worlds — for I am never sated of hearing.
verses.text_note: The translation of this verse was missing in the source dataset; it is taken from the Sivananda text in the gita/gita dataset.
verses.hook: Who alone truly knows God?

refs.note: Nothing surpasses God; He is beyond everything, supporting Arjuna's titles for Him as Lord of all.

views.text: He alone knows himself, and by himself, needing no other means. Arjuna piles up names out of deep reverence, and each name gives a reason why he is the highest Person.
He is Purushottama because he takes four roles: source of beings, their Lord, God of gods, and ruler of the world. As ruler he guides people through the teaching of the Vedas.
Finite minds cannot know the infinite, and this exalts God; only He knows Himself, and a soul He chooses to empower comes to know Him too.

verses.devanagari:
वक्तुमर्हस्यशेषेण दिव्या ह्यात्मविभूतयः ।
याभिर्विभूतिभिर्लोकानिमांस्त्वं व्याप्य तिष्ठसि॥
verses.transliteration:
vaktumarhasyaśeṣeṇa divyā hyātmavibhūtayaḥ
yābhirvibhūtibhirlokānimāṃstvaṃ vyāpya tiṣṭhasi
verses.essence: Please describe without remainder your divine self-manifestations — the pervading powers by which you abide, filling all these worlds.
verses.translation: Thou shouldst indeed tell, without reserve, of Thy divine glories by which Thou existest, pervading all these worlds. (None else can do so.)

anvaya.form: adjective used as adverb, instrumental singular (completely)
anvaya.parts: अ (without) + शेष (remainder): leaving nothing out
आत्मन् (your own self) + विभूति (glory): the glories of your own self

anvaya.form: relative pronoun, feminine, instrumental plural (by which)

verses.explanation: The formal request that generates the rest of the chapter: tell me your vibhūtis — where, in this teeming world, the divine current runs closest to the surface. Arjuna is asking for handholds: the infinite is unclimbable; its outcroppings are not.
verses.connection: Commissions the great catalogue of 10.20–39.
verses.reflection: Ask sincerely to be shown the divine glories in your own ordinary rooms today.
verses.background: Arjuna responds — the first time in the poem he confesses full faith: You are the supreme Brahman, declared so by Narada, Asita, Devala, Vyasa, and now by Yourself; neither gods nor demons know Your manifestation. Then the request that shapes the chapter: tell me Your divine glories, by which You pervade the worlds — for I am never sated of hearing.
verses.hook: What does Arjuna ask Krishna to describe next?

views.text: Arjuna asks the Lord to describe in full his own divine manifestations of glory, through which he exists pervading all these worlds.
Only he can reveal these glories. Each vibhūti shows his will to rule, and through them he abides in all the worlds as their controller.
Having understood that Krishna is the Supreme Lord, Arjun asks to hear His divine glories in creation so his devotion may become unshakeable, knowing such revelation needs Krishna's grace.

verses.devanagari:
कथं विद्यामहं योगिंस्त्वां सदा परिचिन्तयन् ।
केषु केषु च भावेषु चिन्त्योऽसि भगवन्मया॥
verses.transliteration:
kathaṃ vidyāmahaṃ yogiṃstvāṃ sadā paricintayan
keṣu keṣu ca bhāveṣu cintyo'si bhagavanmayā
verses.essence: How may I know you, O Yogi, by constant meditation? And in what various states of being are you to be contemplated by me, Lord?
verses.translation: How shall I, ever meditating, know Thee, O Yogin? In what aspects or things, O blessed Lord, art Thou to be thought of by me?

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, nominative singular (while meditating)
interrogative pronoun, masculine, locative plural (repeated: in which various)
gerundive, masculine, nominative singular (must be thought of)

verses.explanation: The practical heart of the request: keṣu keṣu bhāveṣu — in which things, exactly? Arjuna wants a meditator's field guide: not a doctrine of omnipresence but a list of places where omnipresence shows. The mind cannot grip 'everywhere'; it can grip the sun, the lion, the Ganga.
verses.connection: Refines 10.16 into the chapter's true genre: a contemplative's gazetteer.
verses.reflection: Pick your forms for meditating today — Arjuna's question is yours: in what aspects shall I think of You?
verses.background: Arjuna responds — the first time in the poem he confesses full faith: You are the supreme Brahman, declared so by Narada, Asita, Devala, Vyasa, and now by Yourself; neither gods nor demons know Your manifestation. Then the request that shapes the chapter: tell me Your divine glories, by which You pervade the worlds — for I am never sated of hearing.
verses.hook: How can you keep thinking of the Divine in everyday life?

views.text: Yogi here means one who has the fruits of yoga, omniscience and omnipotence. Arjuna asks through which objects he should meditate on such a Lord.
'Yogin' here refers to Arjuna himself: I, your devotee given to bhakti-yoga. He asks in what further modes, beyond the dispositions already listed, the Lord is to be meditated on.
If he knows the glories in detail, Arjuna can meditate on the Lord even when his mind is drawn to outer objects, seeing him in each, and so behold oneness everywhere.
Arjuna now sees Krishna as the Supreme Lord and asks which of his glories to dwell on, so that his devotion becomes steady; yet he knows such revelation comes only by Krishna's grace.

verses.devanagari:
विस्तरेणात्मनो योगं विभूतिं च जनार्दन ।
भूयः कथय तृप्तिर्हि शृण्वतो नास्ति मेऽमृतम्॥
verses.transliteration:
vistareṇātmano yogaṃ vibhūtiṃ ca janārdana
bhūyaḥ kathaya tṛptirhi śṛṇvato nāsti me'mṛtam
verses.essence: Tell me again, in full, your yoga and your pervading glory, Janardana — for I am never sated of hearing this nectar.
verses.translation: Tell me again in detail, O Krishna, of Thy Yogic power and glory; for I am not satiated with what I have heard of Thy life-giving and nectar-like speech.

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, instrumental singular (as adverb: in detail)

anvaya.base: जनार्दन · Kṛṣṇa, the one people pray to
anvaya.parts: जन (people) + अर्दन (one who is entreated, or who drives away): he whom people pray to

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, genitive singular (of one hearing)
noun, neuter, accusative singular (object of hearing)

verses.explanation: The listener's confession that licenses the longest answer in the chapter: amṛtam — this is nectar, and nectar has no fill-line. Tṛptir nāsti: the appetite that grows by feeding, the one hunger the Gita everywhere approves. Teaching flows where thirst like this waits.
verses.connection: Completes the petition (10.12–18); the floodgates of the catalogue open next.
verses.reflection: Hear the nectar past fullness once: ask for more of what genuinely nourishes, unashamed.
verses.background: Arjuna responds — the first time in the poem he confesses full faith: You are the supreme Brahman, declared so by Narada, Asita, Devala, Vyasa, and now by Yourself; neither gods nor demons know Your manifestation. Then the request that shapes the chapter: tell me Your divine glories, by which You pervade the worlds — for I am never sated of hearing.
verses.hook: Why does hearing about the Divine leave you wanting more, not less?

refs.note: The sages of Naimiṣāraṇya say devotees never tire of hearing the Lord's pastimes; the more they relish them, the sweeter they grow, just as Arjuna's thirst is not quenched.

views.text: Janārdana is read two ways: the one who drives the demons, enemies of the gods, to hell, or the one whom all beings entreat for prosperity and liberation.
Arjuna asks to hear in full what was said only briefly in 10.8, that the Lord is the origin from whom all proceeds: his creative power and his rule.
The detail is wanted so that even a mind turned outward will think of the Lord in each thing it meets, through his particular glories.
Words about God's glories are nectar to those who love him: they satisfy and at once increase the thirst, which is why Arjuna begs Krishna to keep speaking.

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
हन्त ते कथयिष्यामि दिव्या ह्यात्मविभूतयः ।
प्राधान्यतः कुरुश्रेष्ठ नास्त्यन्तो विस्तरस्य मे॥
verses.transliteration:
hanta te kathayiṣyāmi divyā hyātmavibhūtayaḥ
prādhānyataḥ kuruśreṣṭha nāstyanto vistarasya me
verses.essence: Yes — I shall recount to you my divine self-manifestations, but only the chief of them, best of Kurus; for there is no end to my extent.
verses.translation: Very well! Now I will declare to thee My divine glories in their prominence, O Arjuna; there is no end to their detailed description.

anvaya.form: noun compound, feminine, nominative plural (what is to be told)
anvaya.parts: आत्मन् (my own self) + विभूति (glory): the glories of myself

anvaya.meaning: by their eminence, the chief ones

anvaya.parts: कुरु (the Kuru line) + श्रेष्ठ (best): the finest of the Kurus

verses.explanation: Hanta — the warm exclamation of a teacher delighted to be asked. Then the honest disclaimer that frames everything to come: prādhānyataḥ, only headline entries; the full inventory has no last page. The catalogue is a sampler, not a census — finite windows cut into an infinite wall.
verses.connection: Accepts 10.16–18's commission with its terms: highlights only, for the whole is endless.
verses.reflection: Accept the summary nature of all teaching — the detail is endless; let the chief glories suffice today.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Can anyone ever describe all of God's glories?

refs.note: Calls God infinite, manifesting in countless forms while remaining the non-doer, supporting Krishna's word that his glories have no end.
Says God is unlimited and so are the stories of his many descents, echoing that no full account is possible.
One might count the dust of the earth, but whoever thinks he can count God's glories has a childish mind; hence Krishna names only the chief ones.

views.text: They could not be told in full even in a hundred years, so he names those that are pre-eminent, each in its own sphere.
To be a vibhūti is to be under the Lord's control. He rules every creature from within as its Self, and that is why each can be named as him.
Hanta is an address of compassion. Since the sub-glories are endless, he will describe only a few of the principal ones.
Everything about God is unlimited: his forms, names, abodes and glories. So Krishna will describe only a small, prominent fraction of his powers.

verses.devanagari:
अहमात्मा गुडाकेश सर्वभूताशयस्थितः ।
अहमादिश्च मध्यं च भूतानामन्त एव च॥
verses.transliteration:
ahamātmā guḍākeśa sarvabhūtāśayasthitaḥ
ahamādiśca madhyaṃ ca bhūtānāmanta eva ca
verses.essence: I am the Self, Gudakesha, seated in the heart of all beings; I am the beginning, the middle, and the very end of beings.
verses.translation: I am the Self, O Gudakesa, seated in the hearts of all beings; I am the beginning, the middle and also the end of all beings.

anvaya.parts: गुडाका (sleep) + ईश (master): one who has mastered sleep (or, one with thick hair)

anvaya.meaning: seated in the hearts of all beings
anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + भूत (beings) + आशय (heart, seat) + स्थित (seated): seated in the heart of all beings

verses.explanation: The catalogue's first entry is deliberately its deepest: before sun or lion or Ganga, I am the ātmā seated in the heart of every being, including the one now listening, and the beginning, middle and end of all beings. Śaṅkara makes the order practical: meditate on him first as the inner Self, and whoever cannot should seek him through the glories that follow. Whoever forgets the rest of the list but holds this line has the whole chapter; every later glory is this nearness, made visible outside.
verses.connection: The master-key issued before the catalogue: all outer vibhutis are footnotes to the indwelling one.
verses.reflection: Practice the first vibhuti everywhere: greet the Self seated in the heart of each being you meet.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Where is God in relation to your own self?

refs.note: Defines God as that from which beings are born, by which they live, and into which they return, matching beginning, middle and end.
Calls the Lord the soul of the souls of all embodied beings, as Krishna says he dwells in every heart.
Shukadev explains the gopīs' love by saying Krishna is the Supreme Soul of all beings, appearing in human form.

views.text: He is the indwelling Self, always to be meditated on as such. Whoever cannot do so should meditate on him through the aspects that follow, beginning with origin, continuance and dissolution.
All beings are his body and he is their Self, their support and controller. That indwelling is the ground for every 'I am X' statement in the catalogue that follows.
First he names his sovereign form: the Supreme Self dwelling in every inner organ as its controller, with omniscience and other powers, the cause of the birth, life and end of all beings.
God is closer than the closest, seated within the soul and lending it consciousness and eternity; he is the source, sustainer and final goal of every being.

verses.devanagari:
आदित्यानामहं विष्णुर्ज्योतिषां रविरंशुमान् ।
मरीचिर्मरुतामस्मि नक्षत्राणामहं शशी॥
verses.transliteration:
ādityānāmahaṃ viṣṇurjyotiṣāṃ raviraṃśumān
marīcirmarutāmasmi nakṣatrāṇāmahaṃ śaśī
verses.essence: Of the Adityas I am Vishnu; of lights, the radiant sun; of the Maruts I am Marichi; among the stars I am the moon.
verses.translation: Among the (twelve) Adityas, I am Vishnu; among luminaries, the radiant sun; I am Marichi among the (seven or forty-nine) Maruts; among stars the moon am I.

anvaya.form: proper noun, masculine, nominative singular (subject complement)

anvaya.base: मरीचि · Marīci, chief of the Maruts
anvaya.form: proper noun, masculine, nominative singular (subject complement)

verses.explanation: The pattern is set: in every class, the member where the class's essence burns brightest. Among lights, the sun — not because the rest are dark, but because there the principle of light is least veiled. The list teaches a way of seeing: find the summit of anything, and you have found a window.
verses.connection: First entry of the formula that runs to 10.38: 'of each kind, its crown.'
verses.reflection: Find Him today as the brightest of each class you encounter — the sun among lights, to begin.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Among gods, winds, lights and stars, which ones show Krishna's glory?

refs.note: Says all lamps, stars and even the moon cannot end the night, but sunrise does at once, showing why the sun stands for divine glory.

views.text: Among the twelve Ādityas the Lord is the one called Viṣṇu; among luminaries the radiant sun; among the Maruts, Marīci; and among the stars, the moon.
'Among the stars I am the moon' does not pick the moon out as one star among many; the genitive means the moon is lord of the constellations.
The Viṣṇu among the Ādityas is Vāmana. Avatāras appear in the list as glories only to show surpassing power, and the Maruts may be the seven wind groups, Āvaha and the rest.
The Ādityas and Maruts in general are ordinary manifestations; Viṣṇu, the sun, Marīci and the moon are special ones with greater splendour. Meditate on the sun and moon as forms of the Lord.
In each group Krishna names the one that best reveals his opulence: Vishnu as Vāmana among Aditi's sons, the sun among lights, the chief wind Marīci, and the moon at night.

verses.devanagari:
वेदानां सामवेदोऽस्मि देवानामस्मि वासवः ।
इन्द्रियाणां मनश्चास्मि भूतानामस्मि चेतना॥
verses.transliteration:
vedānāṃ sāmavedo'smi devānāmasmi vāsavaḥ
indriyāṇāṃ manaścāsmi bhūtānāmasmi cetanā
verses.essence: Of the Vedas I am the Sama Veda; of the gods I am Indra; of the senses I am the mind; in beings I am consciousness.
verses.translation: Among the Vedas I am the Sama-Veda; I am Vasava among the gods; among the senses I am the mind; and I am intelligence among living beings.

anvaya.parts: साम (chant) + वेद (Veda): the Veda made of chants

anvaya.base: वासव · Indra, chief of the Vasus

verses.explanation: Of the Vedas, the one that is sung — scripture at its most musical. Then inward: among the senses, the mind that coordinates them; and in all creatures, cetanā, sheer sentience itself. The catalogue keeps alternating outward and inward, refusing to let the seeker look in only one direction.
verses.connection: The formula turns interior: the divine located in awareness itself.
verses.reflection: Among your senses, find Him as the mind; among your hymns, as the one you actually sing.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Which Veda, god, sense and faculty does Krishna call his own?

refs.note: Calls God the consciousness in conscious beings, supporting Krishna's word that he is the awareness in living creatures.

views.text: The mind is the faculty of reflection and doubt, and cetanā is a function of the intellect, ever present in the body-and-senses, through which Consciousness shows itself.
The Sāmaveda is paramount among the four Vedas and the mind paramount among the eleven senses; in living beings the Lord is the very consciousness by which they are conscious.
The mind counts as the eleventh sense and their chief, because none of the ten organs of knowing and acting can work without it.
The musical Sāma Veda, Indra, the mind as king of the senses, and consciousness all reflect God's power; consciousness itself exists in the soul only by his divine power.

verses.devanagari:
रुद्राणां शङ्करश्चास्मि वित्तेशो यक्षरक्षसाम् ।
वसूनां पावकश्चास्मि मेरुः शिखरिणामहम्॥
verses.transliteration:
rudrāṇāṃ śaṅkaraścāsmi vitteśo yakṣarakṣasām
vasūnāṃ pāvakaścāsmi meruḥ śikhariṇāmaham
verses.essence: Of the Rudras I am Shankara; of yakshas and rakshasas, the lord of wealth; of the Vasus I am fire; of mountain peaks I am Meru.
verses.translation: And, among the Rudras I am Sankara; among the Yakshas and Rakshasas, the Lord of wealth (Kubera); among the Vasus I am Pavaka (fire); and among the (seven) mountains I am the Meru.

anvaya.parts: वित्त (wealth) + ईश (lord): the lord of wealth
यक्ष (yaksha) + रक्षस् (rakshasa): yakshas and rakshasas together

anvaya.base: वसु · Vasu, one of eight gods

verses.explanation: Shankara — the auspicious one, Shiva himself — named as his own vibhūti: the catalogue quietly absorbs even the other great God of the tradition into its embrace. The peaks of every pantheon and landscape are claimed, not as rivals annexed but as facets owned.
verses.connection: The catalogue at its most ecumenical: the divine names of others, gathered in.
verses.reflection: Spot the summit of each small mountain range in your day, and name the summit His.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Among Rudras, Yakshas, elements and mountains, what reveals Krishna?

views.text: Among the eleven Rudras the Lord is Śaṅkara, Kubera among Yakṣas and goblins, Fire among the eight Vasus, and Meru among the peaked mountains.
Rakshasas are grouped with yakshas because they share a fierce nature; Meru is chief among all lofty, peaked things.
The eleven Rudras are read as the ten vital airs and the mind, named for the grief they cause when they leave the body; the Vasus are the elements, sun, moon and stars, with fire their chief.
Shankar among Shiva's forms, Kubera the treasurer, fire that warms the other elements, and the rich mountain Meru each display God's opulence, as wealth marks out a wealthy person.

verses.devanagari:
पुरोधसां च मुख्यं मां विद्धि पार्थ बृहस्पतिम् ।
सेनानीनामहं स्कन्दः सरसामस्मि सागरः॥
verses.transliteration:
purodhasāṃ ca mukhyaṃ māṃ viddhi pārtha bṛhaspatim
senānīnāmahaṃ skandaḥ sarasāmasmi sāgaraḥ
verses.essence: Of priests, Partha, know me as the chief, Brihaspati; of commanders I am Skanda; of lakes and still waters I am the ocean.
verses.translation: And, among the household priests (of kings), O Arjuna, know Me to be the chief, Brihaspati; among the army generals I am Skana; among lakes I am the ocean. '

anvaya.base: पुरोधस् · family priest of a king

anvaya.parts: सेना (army) + नी (leader): one who leads an army

anvaya.base: स्कन्द · Skanda, general of the gods

verses.explanation: Three vocations, three crowns: the priesthood's wisest voice, the general the gods themselves chose, and — among all gathered waters — the sea, into which every river resigns its name. Each is the point where a whole category becomes unmistakable.
verses.connection: Continues the survey through office and element alike.
verses.reflection: Of your inner generals and priests, ask which is Skanda, which Brihaspati — He claims the chiefs.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Among priests, generals and waters, which does Krishna name as himself?

refs.note: There Krishna names Vasiṣṭha, not Bṛhaspati, as chief priest, showing that the object matters less than the divine opulence shining in it.

views.text: Brihaspati is foremost among royal priests because he is the priest of Indra himself; sarasām means natural reservoirs, among which the sea is greatest.
Brihaspati is chief as priest of the gods and Skanda as commander of the gods' army; the ocean is chief among bodies of still water.
Because Krishna names different chief priests in different scriptures, the point is not the object itself but God's glory manifesting through it.

verses.devanagari:
महर्षीणां भृगुरहं गिरामस्म्येकमक्षरम् ।
यज्ञानां जपयज्ञोऽस्मि स्थावराणां हिमालयः॥
verses.transliteration:
maharṣīṇāṃ bhṛgurahaṃ girāmasmyekamakṣaram
yajñānāṃ japayajño'smi sthāvarāṇāṃ himālayaḥ
verses.essence: Of the great sages I am Bhrigu; of utterances, the single syllable Om; of sacrifices I am the sacrifice of silent repetition; of immovable things, the Himalaya.
verses.translation: Among the great sages I am Bhrigu; among words I am the one syllable (Om); among sacrifices I am the sacrifice of silent repetition; among the immovable things I am the Himalayas.

anvaya.parts: महा (great) + ऋषि (seer): the great seers
जप (repeating a mantra) + यज्ञ (sacrifice): the sacrifice that is japa
हिम (snow) + आलय (abode): the abode of snow

verses.explanation: Among all sacrifices, the quietest: japa, the whispered or silent repetition that needs no fire, fee, or priest — ranked here above every grand altar. The verse pairs it with Om, speech reduced to seed, and the Himalaya, mass become stillness: three forms of the same monumental quiet.
verses.connection: A verse the contemplative traditions treasured: interiority crowned over spectacle.
verses.reflection: Of all your utterances today, let one be the single syllable; of your offerings, the silent repetition.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Which sage, sound, offering and mountain show Krishna's glory?

refs.note: Says that in the age of Kali, chanting and remembering God's names is the strongest means of crossing worldly existence, praising the japa offering.

views.text: 'Words' is taken as utterances, among which the Lord is the single syllable Om; among rituals he is the japa-yajña, the ritual of repetition, and among immovables the Himalaya.
Words are sounds that convey meaning, and among them the single-lettered Praṇava is the Lord; japa is the most prominent of all sacrificial offerings.
Japa involves neither injury nor loss, so it is the best of sacrifices; Manu is cited that a Brahmin attains salvation by japa alone.
Chanting God's names is the simplest offering, bound by no rules, possible anywhere and more purifying than ritual sacrifice, which is why Krishna names it among his glories.

verses.devanagari:
अश्वत्थः सर्ववृक्षाणां देवर्षीणां च नारदः ।
गन्धर्वाणां चित्ररथः सिद्धानां कपिलो मुनिः॥
verses.transliteration:
aśvatthaḥ sarvavṛkṣāṇāṃ devarṣīṇāṃ ca nāradaḥ
gandharvāṇāṃ citrarathaḥ siddhānāṃ kapilo muniḥ
verses.essence: Of all trees I am the ashvattha; of the divine sages, Narada; of the gandharvas, Chitraratha; of the perfected ones, the sage Kapila.
verses.translation: Among all the trees ( I am) the Peepul; among the divine sages, I am Narada; among Gandharvas, Chitraratha; among the perfected, the sage Kapila.

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + वृक्ष (tree): all the trees

anvaya.base: देवर्षि · seer who is a god
anvaya.parts: देव (god) + ऋषि (seer): gods who are also seers
चित्र (bright, many-coloured) + रथ (chariot): he whose chariot is bright

verses.explanation: The sacred fig under which seekers have always sat; Narada, the wandering singer who carries devotion between worlds; the gandharvas' master musician; Kapila, the philosopher counted born-perfect. Roots, song, and insight — the catalogue's range in a single verse.
verses.connection: The ashvattha planted here will return, inverted, as chapter 15's opening image.
verses.reflection: Notice the best tree, the best sage, the best song you meet today — vibhuti-spotting as a walk.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Which tree, sage, singer and perfected one does Krishna name?

views.text: Divine seers are gods who became seers by seeing Vedic mantras; the perfected are those born already rich in virtue, knowledge and renunciation, and Kapila is chief among them.
The ashvattha is singled out because it is the tree worthy of worship.
A muni is one who practises manana, steady reflection; the siddhas gained virtue, Self-knowledge, dispassion and lordship at birth without effort.
The shade-giving peepul, Nārada who guides great souls by stirring self-reflection, the singer Chitraratha, and Kapila, an Avatār who taught Sānkhya and devotion, each best reveal God's glory.

verses.devanagari:
उच्चैःश्रवसमश्वानां विद्धि माममृतोद्भवम् ।
ऐरावतं गजेन्द्राणां नराणां च नराधिपम्॥
verses.transliteration:
uccaiḥśravasamaśvānāṃ viddhi māmamṛtodbhavam
airāvataṃ gajendrāṇāṃ narāṇāṃ ca narādhipam
verses.essence: Of horses know me as Uchchaihshravas, born of the nectar; of lordly elephants, Airavata; and among men, the king.
verses.translation: Know Me as Ucchaisravas born of nectar, among horses; among lordly elephants (I am) the Airavata; and, among men, the king.

anvaya.parts: उच्चैः (high, loud) + श्रवस् (ear, fame): the high-eared or loud-neighing one
अमृत (nectar of immortality) + उद्भव (origin): one whose origin is the nectar(-churning)

anvaya.base: ऐरावत · Indra's elephant, son of Iravati

anvaya.parts: गज (elephant) + इन्द्र (lord): lords among elephants
नर (men) + अधिप (ruler): the ruler of men

verses.explanation: Two beasts that rose from the churned ocean of immortality — the white horse of heaven, Indra's own elephant — and then, among humans, simply: the king. Wherever sovereignty genuinely sits, the verse says, something of his sits in it; authority at its truest is borrowed radiance.
verses.connection: Royalty in animal and human form: the splendor of rule traced to its lender.
verses.reflection: Among horses, elephants and rulers, the excellence is His — honor one excellent creature and one rightful authority today.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Among horses, elephants and people, where does Krishna's glory appear?

views.text: Amṛtodbhava means born when the ocean was churned for nectar; Airāvata is named as the son of Irāvatī, with 'know Me to be' carried over to each entry.
'Nectar-born' applies to Airāvata as well as to the horse, since both rose from the churning of the milk ocean.
Krishna keeps naming the most magnificent in each class: Indra's swift white horse born from the churning of the ocean, Indra's white elephant Airāvata, and among people the king.

verses.devanagari:
आयुधानामहं वज्रं धेनूनामस्मि कामधुक् ।
प्रजनश्चास्मि कन्दर्पः सर्पाणामस्मि वासुकिः॥
verses.transliteration:
āyudhānāmahaṃ vajraṃ dhenūnāmasmi kāmadhuk
prajanaścāsmi kandarpaḥ sarpāṇāmasmi vāsukiḥ
verses.essence: Of weapons I am the thunderbolt; of cows, the wish-fulfilling Kamadhuk; as progenitor I am Kandarpa, the god of love; of serpents I am Vasuki.
verses.translation: Among weapons I am the thunderbolt; among cows I am the wish-fulfilling cow called Kamadhenu; I am the progenitor, the god of love; among serpents I am Vasuki.

anvaya.parts: काम (wish) + धुक् (milking, from √दुह्): she who yields every wish as milk

verses.explanation: The thunderbolt forged from a sage's bones; the cow that milks whatever is wished; and — startlingly — Kandarpa, desire itself in its generative office, the love that continues the world. Eros, in its dharmic channel (7.11's promise kept), stands in the divine inventory beside the holiest relics.
verses.connection: Echoes 7.11: rightful desire as divine presence, here named as the love-god himself.
verses.reflection: Of weapons, desires, serpents — even your dangerous capacities have a consecrated best. Find yours.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Which weapon, cow, desire and serpent stand for Krishna's power?

views.text: The vajra is the weapon made of the sage Dadhīci's bones; kāmadhuk is Vasiṣṭha's wish-yielding cow, or any cow that gives milk at all times.
Sarpas are single-headed snakes while nāgas (in the next verse) are many-headed; Kandarpa is named as the cause of progeny.
Only desire as the cause of offspring is His glory; desire aimed at mere pleasure is not, being outside scriptural sanction. Sarpas here are the venomous serpents.
The thunderbolt made from sage Dadhīci's bones honours supreme sacrifice. The force of love, Kāma, comes from God and is holy when used to beget good children, not for mere pleasure.

verses.devanagari:
अनन्तश्चास्मि नागानां वरुणो यादसामहम् ।
पितॄणामर्यमा चास्मि यमः संयमतामहम्॥
verses.transliteration:
anantaścāsmi nāgānāṃ varuṇo yādasāmaham
pitṝṇāmaryamā cāsmi yamaḥ saṃyamatāmaham
verses.essence: Of the nagas I am Ananta; of water-beings I am Varuna; of the ancestors I am Aryama; of the subduers I am Yama.
verses.translation: I am Ananta among the Nagas; I am Varuna among water-deities; Aryaman among the Manes I am; I am Yama among the governors.

anvaya.parts: अन् (not) + अन्त (end): the endless one

anvaya.base: वरुण · Varuna, lord of the waters
अर्यमन् · Aryaman, king of the ancestors
यम · Yama, lord of death and law

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, genitive plural (of those who …)

verses.explanation: Ananta, the endless serpent on whom Vishnu rests; the old sea-sovereign; the chief of the fathers — and Yama, death-as-judge, named without flinching among the glories. Even the power that ends lives is, rightly seen, his order-keeping face (9.19 already said as much).
verses.connection: The catalogue's shadow-entries: restraint and death claimed as calmly as light.
verses.reflection: Even among the binders and the dead, He is chief — fear one fewer category today.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Among serpents, water gods, ancestors and rulers, who reflects Krishna?

views.text: Ananta is king of a particular species of snakes, Varuṇa king of the water gods, Aryamā king of the manes, and Yama chief among those who maintain law and order.
Nāgas are the non-venomous serpents, whose king Ananta is Śeṣa; saṃyamatām means those who enforce discipline, among whom Yama is chief.
Yama is the witness of every being's acts, who keeps account of good and bad deeds.
Ananta, who praises God with countless hoods and never finishes, and Yama, who dispenses justice without deviating from his hard duty, both reflect God's glory.

verses.devanagari:
प्रह्लादश्चास्मि दैत्यानां कालः कलयतामहम् ।
मृगाणां च मृगेन्द्रोऽहं वैनतेयश्च पक्षिणाम्॥
verses.transliteration:
prahlādaścāsmi daityānāṃ kālaḥ kalayatāmaham
mṛgāṇāṃ ca mṛgendro'haṃ vainateyaśca pakṣiṇām
verses.essence: Of the daityas I am Prahlada; of reckoners I am Time; of beasts I am the lion; of birds, Garuda, son of Vinata.
verses.translation: And, I am Prahlada among the demons, among the reckoners I am time; among beasts I am the lion, and Vainateya (Garuda) among birds.

anvaya.base: प्रह्लाद · Prahlada, the devotee among demons

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, genitive plural (of those who …)

anvaya.parts: मृग (beast) + इन्द्र (lord): the lord of beasts

verses.explanation: The most moving entry in the list: among the demons themselves, Prahlada — the daitya child whose devotion no torture could extinguish. Even in the lineage defined by opposition to God, God claims his own. No camp, the verse implies, is beyond having a saint.
verses.connection: Grace inside the enemy line: the catalogue refuses to concede any territory entirely.
verses.reflection: Among the devious and the counters of time, His glory still indexes — nothing is outside the catalog.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Which demon, beast and bird does Krishna name as his glory?

views.text: 'Kalayatām' is read as those who calculate, so the Lord is Time among reckoners; the king of beasts may be the lion or the tiger; Prahlāda is chief among Diti's descendants.
Kalayatām is taken as those who reckon with intent to harm, and Kāla here as death, meaning the emissary of Yama who records each creature's time of death.
Kalayatām can mean either those who subdue or those who count; in both senses Time is chief.
Prahlāda, though son of the demon Hiraṇyakaśipu, was a great devotee of the Lord.
Prahlāda, a great devotee born among demons, best reflects God's glory there; time wears down even the mightiest; the lion and Garuḍa lead the beasts and birds.

verses.devanagari:
पवनः पवतामस्मि रामः शस्त्रभृतामहम् ।
झषाणां मकरश्चास्मि स्रोतसामस्मि जाह्नवी॥
verses.transliteration:
pavanaḥ pavatāmasmi rāmaḥ śastrabhṛtāmaham
jhaṣāṇāṃ makaraścāsmi srotasāmasmi jāhnavī
verses.essence: Of purifiers I am the wind; of weapon-bearers I am Rama; of fishes I am the makara; of rivers I am the Ganga.
verses.translation: Among the purifiers (or the speeders) I am the wind; Rama among the warriors am I; among the fishes I am the shark; among the streams I am the Ganga.

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, genitive plural (of those who …)

anvaya.parts: शस्त्र (weapon) + भृत् (bearing): those who bear weapons

anvaya.base: जाह्नवी · daughter of Jahnu, the Ganga

verses.explanation: Rama — the other great avatara, dharma with a bow — named by Krishna as himself: one descent saluting another across the ages. Beside him, the wind that cleanses by passing through, and the river that has carried more prayers than any water on earth.
verses.connection: Avatara recognizing avatara: the catalogue's quiet self-reference.
verses.reflection: Be the Ganga among your own rivers today: the version of your work that purifies as it flows.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Among purifiers, warriors, fish and rivers, what is Krishna?

views.text: 'Pavatām' means purifiers, among whom the Lord is air; the Rāma named among weapon-bearers is the son of Daśaratha; the makara is a shark; among streams he is the Gaṅgā.
Since Rāma is the Lord himself, the glory named here is the quality of bearing weapons; the other entries are selves forming the Lord's body.
Pavatām means purifiers or the swift; Rāma may be Dāśarathi or Paraśurāma; the makara is a particular great fish, timiṅgila.
Gaṅgā is called Jāhnavī because the sage Jahnu swallowed her as Bhagīratha was bringing her down from heaven.
Wind purifies nature; Rāma was the mightiest warrior yet never misused his power, and was an Avatār; the Ganges flows from the Lord's feet and is holy.

verses.devanagari:
सर्गाणामादिरन्तश्च मध्यं चैवाहमर्जुन ।
अध्यात्मविद्या विद्यानां वादः प्रवदतामहम्॥
verses.transliteration:
sargāṇāmādirantaśca madhyaṃ caivāhamarjuna
adhyātmavidyā vidyānāṃ vādaḥ pravadatāmaham
verses.essence: Of creations I am the beginning, the end, and also the middle, Arjuna; of sciences, the science of the Self; of those who debate, I am the reasoned discourse.
verses.translation: Among creations I am the beginning, the middle and also the end, O Arjuna; among the sciences I am the science of the Self; and I am the logic among controversialists.

anvaya.parts: अध्यात्म (concerning the Self) + विद्या (knowledge): knowledge whose subject is the Self

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, genitive plural (of those who …)

verses.explanation: Among all branches of knowledge, the one that studies the knower; and among all modes of argument, vāda — debate conducted to find truth rather than to win (the tradition distinguished it sharply from mere wrangling). Even disagreement, done honestly, is a place he lives.
verses.connection: Knowledge and honest argument enrolled: the intellect's best uses as vibhuti.
