verses.reflection: Of all your studies, return to the science of the Self today — vidyas crowned by adhyatma-vidya.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Among all kinds of knowledge, which does Krishna call his own?

refs.note: Lists the fourteen, or eighteen, branches of learning, against which Krishna sets spiritual knowledge as the highest.
Says true knowledge is that which attaches the intellect to God's feet, explaining why the science of the self is supreme.

views.text: In 10.20 beginning, middle and end referred to conscious beings; here they cover all creation. Self-knowledge is foremost because it leads to liberation, and vāda because it settles the true meaning, unlike jalpa or vitaṇḍā.
At every moment the Lord is the creator of what is being created, the sustainer of what is sustained and the destroyer of what is destroyed.
Vāda is the discussion of seekers free of attachment, aversion and jealousy who question each other to find truth, not to win.

Krishna is the creator, sustainer and destroyer of all creation. Of all learning, spiritual knowledge is highest because it frees from bondage, and the logic that lets truth be established also shows his power.

verses.devanagari:
अक्षराणामकारोऽस्मि द्वन्द्वः सामासिकस्य च ।
अहमेवाक्षयः कालो धाताहं विश्वतोमुखः॥
verses.transliteration:
akṣarāṇāmakāro'smi dvandvaḥ sāmāsikasya ca
ahamevākṣayaḥ kālo dhātāhaṃ viśvatomukhaḥ
verses.essence: Of letters I am the letter A; of compounds, the dvandva; I alone am inexhaustible Time; I am the Ordainer facing every direction.
verses.translation: Among the letters of the alphabets, the letter 'A' I am and the dual among the compounds. I am verily the inexhaustible or everlasting time; I am the dispenser (of the fruits of actions) having faces in all directions.

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, neuter, genitive singular (of/among)

anvaya.parts: विश्वतः (on all sides) + मुख (face): one whose faces are everywhere

verses.explanation: The first vowel, latent in every consonant — speech's hidden ground; and among grammatical compounds, the dvandva, where both members keep equal weight: even grammar's most egalitarian form is noted. Then the scale leaps: akṣayaḥ kālaḥ, Time that does not run out — the second naming of Time, now as endurance rather than reckoning.
verses.connection: From the smallest unit of language to duration itself — the catalogue's widest single span.
verses.reflection: Watch Time today as undecaying — and the Dispenser facing every direction, including yours.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Which letter, word form and creator reveal Krishna?

views.text: Kāla is time made of moments, or else the supreme God who is the measurer even of time.
'A' is the base of all letters, as the Aitareya Āraṇyaka says that 'a' is all speech; the dvandva is eminent because both its members carry equal weight; dhātā is the four-faced Hiraṇyagarbha.
Imperishable time is time as an unbroken flow, unlike the 'time of reckoners' in 10.30, which is a measured lifespan that runs out; dhātā is the one who allots the fruits of all actions.
The letter A underlies every Sanskrit syllable; the dvandva compound keeps both words prominent, as in Radha-Krishna; and Brahmā's creative power best reflects God among creators.

verses.devanagari:
मृत्युः सर्वहरश्चाहमुद्भवश्च भविष्यताम् ।
कीर्तिः श्रीर्वाक्च नारीणां स्मृतिर्मेधा धृतिः क्षमा॥
verses.transliteration:
mṛtyuḥ sarvaharaścāhamudbhavaśca bhaviṣyatām
kīrtiḥ śrīrvākca nārīṇāṃ smṛtirmedhā dhṛtiḥ kṣamā
verses.essence: I am all-seizing death, and the origin of all that is to come; among feminine powers: fame, fortune, speech, memory, intelligence, constancy and patience.
verses.translation: And I am the all-devouring Death, and the prosperity of those who are to be prosperous; among the feminine qualities (I am) fame, prosperity, speech, memory, intelligence, firmness and forgiveness.

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + हर (taking away): one who takes away all

anvaya.form: future participle, masculine, genitive plural (of those who will be)

verses.explanation: The bluntest line in the catalogue — mṛtyuḥ sarva-haraḥ, the death that takes everything — set against udbhava, the springing-up of all futures: one hand closes, the other opens, same owner. Then seven goddesses of the inner life, the powers a person most hopes to keep: all of them named as her, as him.
verses.connection: Death and the future in one breath — the catalogue's refusal to look away, continued from 10.29.
verses.reflection: Hold both honestly: He is death the seizer and the seven graces — fame, fortune, speech, memory among them.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: How are death, birth and the finest human virtues forms of Krishna?

views.text: Death that takes life, as opposed to death that takes wealth, is the all-seizer, or God who withdraws all at dissolution; udbhava is the rise to prosperity of those fit for it. A mere trace of these feminine qualities makes a person feel fulfilled.
Nārīṇām refers to the goddesses who are the Lord's own powers, and udbhava is simply the birth of all who are to be born.
Medhā is the power to hold scriptural teaching; dhṛti keeps body and senses steady amid suffering. Several of these are counted as Daksha's daughters, wives of Dharma.

God is the force of destruction as well as creation, devouring all as death and generating future beings. Fame, prosperity, speech, memory, intelligence, courage and forgiveness are his glories in women.

verses.devanagari:
बृहत्साम तथा साम्नां गायत्री छन्दसामहम् ।
मासानां मार्गशीर्षोऽहमृतूनां कुसुमाकरः॥
verses.transliteration:
bṛhatsāma tathā sāmnāṃ gāyatrī chandasāmaham
māsānāṃ mārgaśīrṣo'hamṛtūnāṃ kusumākaraḥ
verses.essence: Of hymns I am the Brihat-saman; of meters I am the Gayatri; of months, Margashirsha; of seasons, the flower-bearing spring.
verses.translation: Among the hymns also I am the Brihatsaman; among metres Gayatri am I; among the months I am the Margasirsha; among the seasons (I am) the flowery season.

anvaya.parts: बृहत् (great) + सामन् (chant): the great chant

anvaya.base: सामन् · chant of the Sama Veda

anvaya.parts: कुसुम (flower) + आकर (mine, store): the storehouse of flowers

verses.explanation: The Gayatri — the meter of the mantra recited at dawn through the ages; the harvest month when the old year's work is gathered; and kusumākara, spring, the season that makes flowers. The calendar itself has summits, and he claims them.
verses.connection: Time's gentler faces after 10.34's severe ones: the year's song, the year's bloom.
verses.reflection: Of your months and seasons, find the flowering one — and sing one Brihat-sama line of your own.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Which hymn, metre, month and season does Krishna name as his?

refs.note: The Gāyatrī mantra, a prayer to the Lord who lights the worlds to illumine our intellect, shows why the Gāyatrī metre is named.

views.text: Gāyatrī here means the Ṛk composed in the Gāyatrī meter; the month is Mārgaśīrṣa, also called Āgrahāyaṇa.
The Bṛhat-sāman is sung on the verse 'tvām iddhi havāmahe' and praises Indra as lord of all; Gāyatrī is best because it makes one twice-born and fetched the Soma.
Mārgaśīrṣa is temperate, and in olden days the count of the year began with it, so it held first place.
Krishna names the most beloved in each class: the melodious Bṛhatsāma, the Gāyatrī metre, the mild harvest month Mārgaśīrṣa, and spring, king of seasons.

verses.devanagari:
द्यूतं छलयतामस्मि तेजस्तेजस्विनामहम् ।
जयोऽस्मि व्यवसायोऽस्मि सत्त्वं सत्त्ववतामहम्॥
verses.transliteration:
dyūtaṃ chalayatāmasmi tejastejasvināmaham
jayo'smi vyavasāyo'smi sattvaṃ sattvavatāmaham
verses.essence: I am the gambling of the cunning; I am the splendor of the splendid; I am victory, I am resolve; I am the goodness of the good.
verses.translation: I am the gambling of the fraudulent; I am the splendour of the splendid; I am victory; I am determination (of those who are determined); I am the goodness of the good.

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, genitive plural (of those who …)

verses.explanation: The list's most unnerving entry: dyūtam, the dice — the very game in which the Pandavas' kingdom was gambled away, Arjuna and his dignity with it. Even the world's sharp practice draws its cleverness from the one source; nothing, not even what wounded the listener most, runs on independent power. Honesty this complete is the catalogue's deepest claim.
verses.connection: The hardest vibhuti for Arjuna to hear — and proof the list excludes nothing.
verses.reflection: Even the gambler's dice are claimed — let no corner of your day pretend to be outside Him.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: If Krishna is even the gambler's cunning, is gambling then fine?

views.text: Tejas is taken as irresistible power and jaya as the excellence of the excellent; sattva means its fruits — virtue, knowledge and detachment — in those endowed with it.
Dicing is named as the chief device of those who practise fraud to defeat one another; sattva here is magnanimity of mind.
God gives every soul power along with freedom of choice; like a power station, he is not responsible for its misuse. Victory, resolve and goodness come from him, not from us.

verses.devanagari:
वृष्णीनां वासुदेवोऽस्मि पाण्डवानां धनञ्जयः ।
मुनीनामप्यहं व्यासः कवीनामुशना कविः॥
verses.transliteration:
vṛṣṇīnāṃ vāsudevo'smi pāṇḍavānāṃ dhanañjayaḥ
munīnāmapyahaṃ vyāsaḥ kavīnāmuśanā kaviḥ
verses.essence: Of the Vrishnis I am Vasudeva; of the Pandavas, Dhananjaya; of the sages I am Vyasa; of the seers, the poet Ushana.
verses.translation: Among the Vrishnis I am Vaasudeva; among the Pandavas I am Arjuna; among the sages I am Vyasa; among the Poets I am Usanas, the poet.

anvaya.parts: धनम् (wealth) + जय (winning): one who wins wealth

anvaya.base: व्यास · Vyasa, arranger of the Veda

verses.explanation: The catalogue turns and looks at its own audience: among the Pandavas — *you*, Arjuna. The listener discovers himself inside the list of glories he has been hearing; his own excellence was never his private property. And Vyasa: the teller of this very tale, claimed by his own character.
verses.connection: The list's most intimate move: the hearer, and the author, enrolled among the vibhutis.
verses.reflection: Of the Pandavas, Dhananjaya: hear yourself included in the list, and stand a little straighter.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Among his own clan, the Pandavas, sages and poets, who is Krishna?

views.text: Vāsudeva is 'I who am this person, your friend', and Dhananjaya is 'you yourself'; kavi means the omniscient, who know past, present and future.
Here the glory is the very fact of being Vasudeva's son, since no other meaning is possible; munis are those who perceive truth by meditation.
The Vāsudeva meant is the one now teaching Arjuna, and Dhananjaya is Arjuna himself as a glory of the Lord; munis are those devoted to reflecting on the Veda's meaning.
Krishna himself shines in the Vrishni line; Arjuna was his intimate devotee and friend; Vyāsa, an Avatār, gave scripture to the world; and the learned Śukrācārya also reflects God's glory.

verses.devanagari:
दण्डो दमयतामस्मि नीतिरस्मि जिगीषताम् ।
मौनं चैवास्मि गुह्यानां ज्ञानं ज्ञानवतामहम्॥
verses.transliteration:
daṇḍo damayatāmasmi nītirasmi jigīṣatām
maunaṃ caivāsmi guhyānāṃ jñānaṃ jñānavatāmaham
verses.essence: Of punishers I am the rod; of those who seek victory I am statecraft; of secrets I am silence; of the wise I am wisdom.
verses.translation: Of those who punish, I am the sceptre; among those who seek victory, I am statesmanship; and also among secrets, I am silence; knowledge among knowers I am.

anvaya.form: present participle, masculine, genitive plural (of those who …)
present participle, masculine, genitive plural (of those who …)

anvaya.base: मौन · silence, the way of the muni
गुह्य · what is to be hidden (√गुह्, to hide)

verses.explanation: The catalogue's last formula-verse closes a spiral: of all secrets, mauna — silence, the secret that keeps itself — and of all knowers, the knowing in them. The list of words about God ends by bowing to the wordless and to the very light by which any list is read.
verses.connection: The final entries point past the catalogue: silence and knowledge — where enumeration retires.
verses.reflection: Of restraints, the rod; of secrets, silence — practice one noble silence today and call it His.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: In punishment, ambition, secrets and wisdom, where is Krishna found?

views.text: The rod is the means of controlling the lawless; among those seeking conquest the Lord is righteous policy, among secrets silence, and among the knowing, knowledge.
The rod is His glory because by it even the unrestrained become restrained; silence is chief among secrets because no one can know the intent of one who stays silent.
The silence meant is the one born of constant meditation on Brahman, and the knowledge is knowledge of the Self.
Just punishment reforms conduct; victory won by righteous means shows God's power; the best secret is kept in silence; and true wisdom sees everything in relation to God.

verses.devanagari:
यच्चापि सर्वभूतानां बीजं तदहमर्जुन ।
न तदस्ति विना यत्स्यान्मया भूतं चराचरम्॥
verses.transliteration:
yaccāpi sarvabhūtānāṃ bījaṃ tadahamarjuna
na tadasti vinā yatsyānmayā bhūtaṃ carācaram
verses.essence: And whatever is the seed of all beings, Arjuna, that am I. There is no being, moving or unmoving, that could exist without me.
verses.translation: And whatever is the seed of all beings, that also am I, O Arjuna; there is no being, whether moving or unmoving, that can exist without Me.

anvaya.parts: सर्व (all) + भूत (being): all beings

anvaya.form: pronoun, instrumental singular (with विना: without me)

anvaya.parts: चर (moving) + अचर (unmoving): both moving and unmoving

verses.explanation: The closing clause that makes the whole list redundant: bījam — the seed of everything, listed or not. Na tad asti vinā yat syān mayā: nothing exists that could exist without me. The seventy-odd entries were never an inventory of where he is; they were training wheels for seeing that there is no 'where he isn't.'
verses.connection: Dissolves the catalogue into its principle: the highlights were samples of a total presence.
verses.reflection: Test the closing claim on anything you meet: no being, moving or unmoving, exists without Him.
verses.background: Krishna consents — 'hanta, I will tell you My chief glories, for there is no end to My extent' — and the great catalogue unrolls over the silent battlefield: the Self in every heart first, then sun among lights, OM among words, Himalaya among the unmoving, lion among beasts, Ganga among rivers, Arjuna among Pandavas, down to the dice of gamblers and silence among secrets.
verses.hook: Can anything at all exist without Krishna?

views.text: Whatever He withdraws Himself from would lose all substance and become a non-entity; so everything has Him as its essence.
No being exists without Him as its Self, echoing 10.20; this is why every name in the list can stand in apposition to the Lord.
Krishna is both the efficient and the material cause of creation, the seed of every kind of being, so without his power nothing moving or still could exist.

verses.devanagari:
नान्तोऽस्ति मम दिव्यानां विभूतीनां परन्तप ।
एष तूद्देशतः प्रोक्तो विभूतेर्विस्तरो मया॥
verses.transliteration:
nānto'sti mama divyānāṃ vibhūtīnāṃ parantapa
eṣa tūddeśataḥ prokto vibhūtervistaro mayā
verses.essence: There is no end to my divine manifestations, Parantapa. What I have declared is but an indication of my infinite glory.
verses.translation: There is no end to My divine glories, O Arjuna, but this is a brief statement by Me of the particulars of My divine glories.

anvaya.parts: पर (enemy) + तप (scorching): one who scorches enemies

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, nominative singular (has been spoken)

verses.explanation: The honest accounting promised in 10.19 is delivered: uddeśataḥ — by way of pointing, a finger and not the moon. Every catalogue of the infinite is a brochure; the verse files it as such, lest anyone mistake seventy windows for the whole sky.
verses.connection: Bookends 10.19: the sampler closed with its own disclaimer.
verses.reflection: Stop counting today — the glories have no end; the catalog was only ever a training of the eye.
verses.background: The catalogue closes itself: there is no end to My divine manifestations; this was a mere indication. Whatever is glorious, prosperous, or powerful anywhere — know it sprung from a spark of My splendor. But what need of all this detail? I stand sustaining this entire universe with a single fragment of Myself.
verses.hook: Why did Krishna list his glories if they have no end?

views.text: No one can speak or know the limit of the all-pervading God's manifestations; what was given is partial, by way of illustration.
The manifestations are expressions of the Lord's will to rule, divine and auspicious, of which only a few were shown.
Parantapa is read inwardly: one who burns the inner enemies of lust, anger, greed and delusion.
Arjuna asked how to think of Krishna, and the mind is drawn to what is special; so wherever we see splendour we can let it lead our thoughts to God.

verses.devanagari:
यद्यद्विभूतिमत्सत्त्वं श्रीमदूर्जितमेव वा ।
तत्तदेवावगच्छ त्वं मम तेजोंऽशसम्भवम्॥
verses.transliteration:
yadyadvibhūtimatsattvaṃ śrīmadūrjitameva vā
tattadevāvagaccha tvaṃ mama tejoṃśasambhavam
verses.essence: Whatever being is glorious, prosperous or powerful — understand that to have sprung from but a spark of my splendor.
verses.translation: Whatever being there is glorious, prosperous or powerful, that know thou to be a manifestation of a part of My splendour.

anvaya.form: past participle used as adjective, neuter, nominative singular

anvaya.meaning: born of a fraction of splendour
anvaya.base: तेजस् · splendour; अंश · part; सम्भव · origin
anvaya.parts: तेजस् (splendour) + अंश (part) + सम्भव (origin): having a part of My splendour as its source

verses.explanation: The portable version of the entire chapter, issued for use after the list is forgotten: yad yad vibhūtimat sattvam — whatever being carries glory, grace or power, know it sprung from a fragment of My splendor. Wherever you meet excellence — any beauty, any force, any flourishing — read it as tejo-'ṃśa, a spark off the one fire. The master key is handed over at the catalogue's end: once the rule is held, no inventory is needed, and the whole world becomes the catalogue's next page.
verses.connection: The take-home formula: 10.20–39 compressed into one habit of perception.
verses.reflection: Use the master key all day: wherever you see splendor or strength, read one spark of His fire.
verses.background: The catalogue closes itself: there is no end to My divine manifestations; this was a mere indication. Whatever is glorious, prosperous, or powerful anywhere — know it sprung from a spark of My splendor. But what need of all this detail? I stand sustaining this entire universe with a single fragment of Myself.
verses.hook: Where does all greatness and beauty in the world really come from?

views.text: Any object in the world endowed with majesty, prosperity or vigour should be known for certain as having a part of God's power as its source.
Vibhūtimat is the capacity to rule, śrīmat is beauty or wealth, ūrjita is being engaged in auspicious works; tejas is the Lord's power to overcome opposition, of which each is a fraction.
Before closing, the Lord gives the view of duality-in-unity: each excellent being is distinct yet arises from His splendour; full unity comes in the next verse.
For the listener still eager for more, the Lord now states the whole in one stroke: any thing that excels by some quality arises from a share of His power.
Whatever splendour enchants us is only a spark of God's glory, as sound comes not from the speaker but from the current; so God, the source of all glory, should be worshipped.

verses.devanagari:
अथवा बहुनैतेन किं ज्ञातेन तवार्जुन ।
विष्टभ्याहमिदं कृत्स्नमेकांशेन स्थितो जगत्॥
verses.transliteration:
athavā bahunaitena kiṃ jñātena tavārjuna
viṣṭabhyāhamidaṃ kṛtsnamekāṃśena sthito jagat
verses.essence: But what need have you of all this detailed knowledge, Arjuna? I stand, supporting this entire universe with a single fragment of myself.
verses.translation: But, of what avail to thee is the knowledge of all these details, O Arjuna? I exist, supporting this whole world by one part of Myself.

anvaya.parts: एक (one) + अंश (part): a single portion

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, nominative singular (am standing)

verses.explanation: The chapter ends by waving away its own magnificence: atha vā — but really, why all this? Then the sentence that out-scales everything before it: ekāṁśena, with one fragment I hold the whole. All the worlds, all the catalogue, all the glory — a sliver of him; the rest exceeds existence itself. Arjuna's next request, to *see* this, becomes inevitable.
verses.connection: The closing escalation that detonates into chapter 11: hearing is finished; seeing must begin.
verses.reflection: Carry the final compression with you: one fragment of Him sustains all this. Walk inside that fragment.
verses.background: The catalogue closes itself: there is no end to My divine manifestations; this was a mere indication. Whatever is glorious, prosperous, or powerful anywhere — know it sprung from a spark of My splendor. But what need of all this detail? I stand sustaining this entire universe with a single fragment of Myself.
verses.hook: How much of Krishna does this whole universe actually take up?

refs.note: Says the material world is only one part of the Supreme Person, while three parts are his eternal abodes beyond birth and death.

views.text: The universe is one 'foot' of Him, as the Puruṣa Sūkta says; the rest is the unqualified transcendent Reality, which this chapter's meditation finally points to.
With a tiny fraction of His power the Lord upholds the whole universe of sentient and non-sentient things so that none departs from His will in form, existence or activity.
The list was for a seeker who cannot yet contemplate all-pervasiveness; to stop it implying the Lord is only Himalaya and not other things, it ends in absolute unity: all beings are the Lord.
Why bother with limited, piece-by-piece knowledge? See sameness everywhere, for nothing exists apart from Him.
All the unlimited material universes are held within a mere fraction of God; the material creation is only a quarter of his manifestation, the rest being the spiritual realm.
